target_customer: Consumers who wanted a shareable web calendar (free product)
problem: Desktop calendars were hard to share and reach from other computers or phones.
business_model: Free consumer web app, no revenue model documented

founders.name: Justin Kan
founders.background_notes: YC page lists him as former Kiko founder and later Justin.tv and Twitch founder. Education not listed on YC page; a search snippet called both founders Yale graduates (unverified for him).

exit.reason: Founders sold the business by eBay auction after Google Calendar launched; Tucows won the auction on 2006-08-26.

competitors.name: Trumba
competitors.what: Paid web calendar publishing and sharing

competitors.name: Hula (open source)
competitors.what: Open source calendar and mail project

technical_complexity.rationale: A responsive Ajax calendar with sharing, SMS and phone integration was advanced for 2005 browsers but within reach of a small team.

defensibility.rationale: Tucows later called Kiko a feature, not a business; calendars were easy to copy for large providers and nothing locked users in.

takeover_risk_then.outcome: Google Calendar launched in 2006 and was described as largely matched by Kiko and 30 Boxes, which made a standalone calendar hard to sustain.

market_need_then: Online sharing of calendars was a visible gap in 2005, with Ajax reviews in 2005 and 2006 comparing many new web calendars, though reviewers such as Joel Spolsky could not recommend any.

brand_strength.rationale: Kiko got launch coverage at TechCrunch and a very public eBay sale, but the sale story was about the auction, not a brand followed by users.

outcome_analysis: Kiko launched an Ajax calendar in August 2005 to good early reviews but competed against Google Calendar, which arrived in 2006 and matched its features. The founders listed the company on eBay and Tucows won it on 2006-08-26 to bring calendar features to its email platform, a feature purchase rather than a venture outcome. The founders moved on to Justin.tv.
notes: Price of 258,100 reported by GigaOm and others; Tucows write-up does not state it. CB Insights says total raised 50K and a podcast summary says YC gave 15,000: unverified, not recorded as rounds. A search snippet names Matt Fong as a third builder, not listed on YC page, so not recorded as co-founder. Original site kiko.com was sold to Tucows; no current company site fetched. Name origin search returned only generic name pages. Update: CB Insights lists a 50K seed from YC dated June 2005, now recorded as stage other; single database. Dealroom and CB Insights report sale prices of about 250K, not a round.
